title: The Portrait of the Ninth Floor
premise: Ada Sterling is hired to appraise Marrow House, a decaying estate whose ninth floor appears on no blueprint yet registers on every measurement she takes. The house's mirrors lag one second behind reality, and in that stolen second Ada glimpses the family who died there in 1974 still signing an endless contract for their lives. As the lag widens, the house begins counting its residents — doors, breaths, heartbeats — and Ada realizes her own appraisal report is being written into the contract. To survive, she must get the last living heir, twelve-year-old Iris Vane, out before the final signature lands, at the cost of leaving behind the version of herself the mirrors have already claimed. In the end, Ada burns the papers with her own name on them, walks out as the ninth floor collapses into dust, and carries home a scar: her reflection now arrives one second early.
about_author: Rafael Ashgrove is a former building inspector who spent eleven years cataloguing condemned properties across the Rust Belt before turning to horror. He writes in empty houses, insisting that every structure remembers more than its residents do.

chapters.title: The Commission
chapters.summary: POV Ada. A probate lawyer hires Ada to appraise Marrow House before its sale to a developer; the only condition is that she never go to the ninth floor. She arrives with her laser measure and finds the foyer door count off by one. Emotional beat: professional unease disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Square Footage
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Her measurements keep returning impossible numbers — rooms larger inside than out, a staircase that adds four steps each descent. She meets Iris Vane, the taciturn heir living in the east wing with her grandmother Halcyon. Beat: curiosity sharpening into dread.

chapters.title: The Ninth Floor Problem
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Blueprints show eight floors; the elevator panel shows nine. Halcyon warns her, kindly, that the house 'appraises back' — it decides what things are worth. That night Ada hears paper being signed somewhere above her room. Beat: first contact with the wrongness.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: POV Ada. In the hallway mirror, her reflection raises its hand a beat after she does. She tests every mirror in the house; all of them lag exactly one second. Only Iris seems unsurprised. Beat: the horror becomes measurable, which makes it worse.

chapters.title: What Iris Knows
chapters.summary: POV Iris. Iris explains the rule her grandmother enforces: never look at your reflection while it's looking at you. She shows Ada a child's drawing of nine stick figures on nine floors — the ninth figure has Ada's face. Beat: alliance forming between the two survivors-in-waiting.

chapters.title: The Family in the Glass
chapters.summary: POV Ada. The lag stretches to two seconds, long enough for Ada to see the 1974 Vane family in the mirror-world, seated at a table, signing page after page of a contract that never ends. One of them looks up and mouths her name. Beat: recognition — this is a trap with paperwork.

chapters.title: Halcyon's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Halcyon (flashback woven through present). Halcyon reveals she survived 1974 by letting the house take her husband and six children; her signature bought fifty years. Now the contract nears renewal, and the house wants a full count again. Beat: guilt wearing the mask of protection.

chapters.title: The Count Begins
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Doors begin appearing where walls were solid — forty-one, forty-two, forty-three. Each new door opens onto a memory-room staged from Ada's own past. The house isn't haunting her; it's inventorying her. Beat: violation of the self.

chapters.title: Room Forty-Four
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Behind door forty-four is her childhood bedroom, and in it, her mother — dead eleven years — asking why Ada left. Ada nearly stays. Iris pulls her out by the wrist, and the door seals itself, offended. Beat: temptation and rescue; trust deepens.

chapters.title: The Appraisal Drafts Itself
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Her laptop opens overnight and types her own report — except the valuation column lists people: Halcyon, Iris, Ada, each with a price. The developer's offer letter is already stapled to it, dated tomorrow. Beat: the trap closing in bureaucratic language.

chapters.title: Developer's Men
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Two surveyors from the developer arrive to verify figures and refuse to leave. By dusk they've wandered onto the ninth floor, which now exists for anyone the house has counted. Their voices join the chorus upstairs. Beat: stakes made flesh; the house feeds.

chapters.title: Iris Runs
chapters.summary: POV Iris. Terrified, Iris tries to flee alone; the driveway lengthens under her feet until the gate is a horizon away. She returns to find Halcyon calmly setting a third place at dinner. Beat: despair — the house doesn't keep you in, it makes leaving meaningless.

chapters.title: The Terms
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Ada confronts Halcyon, who confesses the escape clause: if the last resident leaves willingly before the final signature, the contract voids. But the house decides willingness, and it has been curdling Halcyon's love into possession. Beat: the plan, and its poisoned condition.

chapters.title: Lag of Five
chapters.summary: POV Ada. The mirrors are five seconds behind now; Ada watches her past selves make choices she's already regretted. In the deepest reflection she sees the ninth floor clearly: a table, nine chairs, ten place settings. The tenth chair is hers. Beat: inevitability pressing down.

chapters.title: Halcyon Signs
chapters.summary: POV Halcyon. Broken by the house's whispers, Halcyon renews the contract early to 'keep Iris safe forever,' not seeing that the signature lists both their names. Ada catches the pen mid-stroke and shatters it. Beat: betrayal, then fracture — Halcyon begins to wake.

chapters.title: The Long Staircase
chapters.summary: POV Ada and Iris alternating. To void the contract they must reach the table on the ninth floor and burn the master page. The staircase now has two hundred steps, each showing a door from Ada's counted memories trying to open. Beat: ascent as ordeal; mother-figure and child against the house.

chapters.title: What the House Offers
chapters.summary: POV Ada. On the landing, the house speaks through her mother's voice, offering a trade: stay, and Iris goes free, whole and remembered. Ada almost signs. Iris says, 'You already left me once. Don't do it the way it wants.' Beat: the theme made explicit — survival at another's price is just corruption.

chapters.title: The Tenth Chair
chapters.summary: POV Ada. They reach the table. The nine Vanes of 1974 sit signing, faces smooth as glass. The tenth chair waits. Ada sits — but instead of signing, she produces her own appraisal, declaring the house worthless, condemned, value zero. The mirrors scream. Beat: climax; fighting bureaucracy with bureaucracy.

chapters.title: Zero Value
chapters.summary: POV Ada. The contract cannot price what she refuses to value; pages blacken and curl. The nine Vanes stand, released, and dissolve into dust that smells like rain. Halcyon appears on the stairs, old and small, whispering her children's names as they pass. Beat: catharsis and grief entwined.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: POV Iris. Iris must walk out willingly — and she does, taking Halcyon's hand, choosing the living over the haunted. The front door count finally matches: one door, opening outward. Behind them the ninth floor folds down through the house like a closing hand. Beat: release; the escape clause honored.

chapters.title: Closing Costs
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Weeks later, Ada files her report; the developer's project collapses in scandal, the land rezoned as unbuildable. She visits Iris and Halcyon in their small apartment, where there are no mirrors at all. Beat: quiet aftermath; the price paid was her certainty about what's real.

chapters.title: One Second Early
chapters.summary: POV Ada. In her own bathroom, Ada's reflection moves before she does — waving hello a heartbeat ahead. She waves back anyway, and smiles when it smiles first. Final line: some houses you carry with you. Beat: resolution with a splinter of unease; survival changed her permanently.
